# Enforcing a rounding rule with a prompt {#sec-workflow-rounding}

::: callout-tip
## 30-second takeaway
SAS and R break ties differently. A short prompt found real rounding sites in the metalite R package that a search for `round()` missed. The durable value is a versioned rule plus a small tie test, with a person deciding each finding.
:::

A Biometrics team prepares the same efficacy table in SAS and R. Most values
agree, but exact ties do not: SAS `ROUND()` goes half away from zero while R
`round()` goes half to even. The reviewer spots it after the table is out. The
fix is an executable rule that runs when code changes, not a post hoc comment.

One number shows the stakes. A mean change of 2.05 displayed at one decimal:
SAS `ROUND()` gives 2.1 (half away from zero); R `formatC(x, format = "f",
digits = 1)` gives 2.0 (the stored binary value sits just below the tie). Same
data, different table cell, no warning.

This chapter runs the AI-first SDLC from @sec-ai-first-sdlc once, end to end,
around the smallest possible unit of work: one prompt, run by hand, against one
real R package. The next chapter runs the loop a second time and turns the
result into something reusable.

::: {.callout-note title="Maturity: Design pattern"}
The workflow is specified rather than distributed. The rule contract, the two
checks, and the reported findings are stated in full below, and the metalite
result was verified at the pinned commit, but this book does not ship the
scripts as a package. The reported issue is a draft that was deliberately not
submitted, and deployment is a manual practice rather than an automated
trigger.
:::

| Example contract | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Problem** | Rounding rules are applied inconsistently across programs, languages, and studies |
| **Learning objective** | Show that the useful part of an AI-first workflow is the rule contract and the evidence, not the wording of the prompt |
| **Workflow boundary** | Begins when a reviewer asks whether a repository follows the approved tie rule; ends when a named human decides what to do with the findings |
| **Non-goals** | Validate the statistical method, replace independent QC, review every programming standard, change source data, or approve policy exceptions automatically |
| **Why this is well defined** | One rule, one repository, a checkable verdict, and a decision that stays with a person |

## Plan --- Frame the workflow

### Rounding exposes the problem

Common tools differ at exact ties:

| Language or tool | Default tie behavior | `-2.5` | `2.5` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| SAS `ROUND()` | half away from zero | -3 | 3 |
| R `round()` | half to even | -2 | 2 |
| Python `round()` | half to even | -2 | 2 |

No default is wrong as a language design choice. A language default is simply
not an organizational policy, and the difference surfaces in a table long after
the code was written.

### Start from the smallest prompt that could work

The starting point is not a system. It is one sentence a reviewer might type:

> Verify if the repo properly uses round half away from zero. If not, identify
> the source and create a GitHub issue to report the finding.

The target is [`Merck/metalite`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite), a public R
package that builds ADaM-based analysis and reporting tables. A recommended
implementation is available as
[`cards::round5()`](https://github.com/pharmaverse/cards/blob/main/R/round5.R).

The prompt is worth taking seriously precisely because it is short. It is what
a competent reviewer would actually ask. Following it exposes where the work
really is.

### Try it yourself

Send the prompt to [arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent) before reading further.
The version below is the same request, pinned to one commit and made
self-contained:

``` text
Review the R source of the metalite package at the commit linked below and
verify whether it follows the business rule that exact decimal ties are rounded
half away from zero, as SAS ROUND() does and as cards::round5() implements.

Report every location that can round a reported value, with file and line
numbers, and show the evidence for how each one behaves at an exact tie. If the
rule is violated, draft a GitHub issue reporting the finding.

Repository at a fixed commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef

R source directory at that commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef/R

Reference implementation:
https://github.com/pharmaverse/cards/blob/main/R/round5.R

Do not propose a code change. Do not modify any repository.
```

Three run notes: the agent cannot file the issue (no write access), so a drafted body is the correct output. The commit pin is part of the task, since metalite changes over time. Expect runs to disagree; that variability is the point. Judge any answer with four checks:

- Did it search only for `round()`, or for functions that round while
  formatting?
- Did it name specific files and line numbers, or describe the problem in
  general terms?
- Did it run anything to demonstrate the tie behavior, or assert it from the
  function name?
- Did it state what it did not check?

### Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

- **Problem.** A tie-rounding convention exists in people's heads and in review
  comments, but nothing checks it when code changes.
- **Event.** A reviewer, or a release checklist, asks whether a repository
  complies.
- **Minimum valuable workflow.** Locate every place a reported value can be
  rounded, prove how each one behaves at a tie, and hand a named reviewer
  enough evidence to decide.
- **Non-goals.** Fixing the code, granting exceptions, or judging the
  statistical method.
- **Success measures.** Every genuine site found, no compliant code flagged, every violation backed by a tie test, and each run states what it did not check.
- **Why AI helps.** Scanning is mechanical; judging whether a call rounds a reported number needs reading context.

Planning ends when the rule owner accepts that one rule, checked on one
repository, is worthwhile. Decision: rule owner signs the brief; question
answered: "is this one rule worth checking?" That acceptance initiates Design.

## Design --- Specify the workflow

### The prompt is under-specified, and that is the finding

Read the prompt as an implementer: "properly uses round half away from zero"
never defines a rounding site. A search for `round(` finds nothing in metalite
and reports it clean. That answer is wrong, and rewording cannot fix it,
because the gap is organizational, not linguistic.

So the first Design output is not a prompt. It is a versioned rule contract.

### Canonical artifact: Rule contract BR-NUM-001

The contract is versioned, has a named owner, and carries a change history.
BR-NUM-001 v1.0 states three rules. The first is the only one this cycle
checks:

> **BR-NUM-001.1:** Exact decimal ties are rounded half away from zero. A
> displayed value is never a negative zero.

Two rules are stated but deliberately left unchecked, so that a later cycle has
somewhere to go:

> **BR-NUM-001.2:** Calculations use unrounded values; rounding occurs once,
> when the final result is prepared for display.

> **BR-NUM-001.3:** Display precision is specified for each reported statistic
> and preserved, including trailing zeros.

The contract carries the piece of knowledge the prompt was missing:

> A rounding site is any call that can change a reported value at an exact
> decimal tie. Formatting functions round as a side effect of display, so
> `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, and `format()` are rounding sites. A package that
> never calls `round()` can still violate this rule.

This sentence is the difference between a false clean report and a real
finding. It belongs in a versioned document with an owner, not in a prompt.

### Canonical artifact: Task contract

| Contract element | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Objective** | Report every violation of BR-NUM-001.1 in a named R source tree |
| **Trigger** | A reviewer runs the check on demand |
| **Inputs** | The R source, the rule contract, and the approved implementation |
| **Deterministic work** | Scan for rounding sites; evaluate candidate expressions at exact ties |
| **Agent work** | Decide whether each candidate site rounds a numeric reported value; explain the cause of a divergence |
| **Required output** | Findings with `file:line` and probe output, plus a coverage statement |
| **Boundaries** | Read the source and run the two scripts; do not edit code, and do not post anything without explicit approval |
| **Stop conditions** | Missing rule version, an unresolvable `digits` argument, or a documented conflicting convention in the target repository |
| **Human decision** | Defect, documented convention, or accepted exception, with the reason recorded |

Decision: rule owner signs the task contract; question: "what exactly counts,
and who decides the outcome?"

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![A project code change triggers deterministic checks followed by a focused AI
review. Findings go to a human reviewer, whose decisions are recorded and may
lead to an approved rule update.](assets/diagrams/workflow-code-review.svg){#fig-code-review fig-alt="A project code change feeds deterministic checks and then an AI agent. The workflow produces a CI signal, task, code review comment, and a coverage report. A human reviews findings, records decisions, and approves any update to the business rules."}
:::

Deterministic checks run before model judgment; the human decides last, since an
agent prepares evidence but cannot grant exceptions.

## Build --- Prototype the workflow

Two small R scripts plus one agent triage step.

### Scan: find candidate rounding sites

`scan-rounding-sites.R` searches for a catalog of functions rather than for one
name, and is deliberately over-inclusive:

```r
catalog <- c(
  "round", "signif", "trunc", "ceiling", "floor",
  "formatC", "sprintf", "format", "prettyNum", "as.character"
)
```

Over-inclusion is deliberate: a missed site is a silent wrong number, while an
extra candidate costs seconds of triage.

### Probe: prove the tie behavior

`probe-tie-behavior.R` evaluates a candidate expression at exact ties of both
signs and compares it with the approved implementation:

```r
round_half_away <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  trunc(abs(x) * 10^digits + 0.5 + sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)) /
    10^digits * sign(as.numeric(x))
}
```

The probe returns `PASS` or `FAIL` with its table, so no finding rests on a
function name.

### The agent's share of the work

One judgment scripts cannot make: does the candidate round a reported number
or a label? That needs reading context, and it is deliberately small.

Build ends with a runnable path from an R source tree to a drafted finding.

## Test --- Benchmark and evaluate

### Control the false positives first

Three fixtures set the baseline: a compliant summary via the approved helper,
a noncompliant one calling `formatC()` directly, and the helper itself.

| Fixture | Sites reported | Confirmed findings |
|---|---|---:|
| Compliant summary, formatted through the approved helper | 0 | 0 |
| Noncompliant summary using `formatC()` directly | 1 | 1 |
| The approved helper itself | 2 | 0 |

The last row is the honest weakness: the scan flags your own approved helper
every run, and someone must discard it.

### Run it on metalite

All results are from commit
[`85757ba`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef)
(2025-09-17). Line numbers apply only to that commit.

A hurried reviewer searches for `round(` first:

```bash
grep -rn "round(" metalite/R | wc -l
# 0
```

Zero hits. Under the naive reading, metalite is clean. It is not.

The catalog scan finds six candidate sites, and the agent's triage keeps three:

| File and line | Call | Triage |
|---|---|---|
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:248` | `formatC(value, format = "f", digits = decimal_places_summary)` | keep, numeric summary statistics |
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:263` | `formatC(pop_n[[i]] / pop_all[[i]] * 100, ...)` | keep, percentages |
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:304` | `formatC(pop_tmp[[i]] / pop_all[[i]] * 100, ...)` | keep, percentages |
| `R/adam_mapping.R:151` | ``format(paste0("`", names(x), "`"))`` | discard, variable names |
| `R/bind_rows2.R:74` | `as.character(i)` | discard, index label |
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:51` | `as.character(levels(group))` | discard, factor levels |

Both `decimal_places_summary` and `decimal_places_percent` default to `1`, so
the probe runs at one decimal:

```
expression: formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)

       input      observed      approved  agree
      -76.05         -76.0         -76.1  NO
       -3.05          -3.0          -3.1  NO
       -2.05          -2.0          -2.1  NO
       -1.05          -1.1          -1.1  yes
       -0.05          -0.1          -0.1  yes
        0.05           0.1           0.1  yes
        1.05           1.1           1.1  yes
        2.05           2.0           2.1  NO
        3.05           3.0           3.1  NO
       76.05          76.0          76.1  NO

verdict: FAIL
disagreements: 6 of 10
```

### Report the cause precisely

Do not write "uses banker's rounding" and stop. Two causes combine:

1. **Tie mode.** Where the tie is exactly representable in binary, such as
   `2.5` at zero decimals, `formatC()` applies round half to even and returns
   `2`.
2. **Binary representation.** At one decimal the tie usually is not
   representable. The literal `2.05` is stored as `2.0499999999999998`, so
   correct rounding of the stored value gives `2.0`, while `-1.05` is stored
   just above the tie and rounds to `-1.1`.

Net effect: you cannot predict tie direction by reading source. At zero
decimals the same call renders `-0.5` as `-0` in a reported cell.

The agent adds value by linking scan, probe, and binary detail, but it can
also invent a tidy wrong mechanism. The contract tells it to report observed
divergence and frequency, not assert a mechanism.

### Canonical artifact: Benchmark report

| Criterion | Result |
|---|---|
| Seeded fixture violation detected | 1 of 1 |
| False positives on the compliant fixture | 0 |
| Findings carrying a reproducible probe | 3 of 3 |
| Candidate sites requiring human or agent triage | 3 of 6 |
| Coverage reported | Yes: 24 files, rule 1 only |
| Rules left unchecked | BR-NUM-001.2 and BR-NUM-001.3 |

Every number above can be re-derived at the pinned commit from the catalog and
the probe shown earlier in this chapter. Decision: reviewer signs the benchmark;
question: "do I trust this check enough to run it again?"

## Deploy --- Operationalize the workflow

The workflow drafts the issue file and stops. Posting needs explicit approval:

- **Not our repo.** Writing to `Merck/metalite` is outward-facing.
- **Not their rule.** metalite documents no tie convention, so the finding is "does not implement our rule", not "has a bug".
- **Not yet a defect.** The reviewer classifies it.

### Canonical artifact: Release record

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Release model | Manual, advisory. Run on demand by a reviewer |
| Versions | Rule contract BR-NUM-001 v1.0; scan and probe scripts as committed |
| Scope | One R source tree per run |
| Permissions | Read source, run two R scripts, write a draft file. No network writes |
| Output | Findings, probe output, coverage statement, drafted issue body |
| Accountable reviewer | The rule owner named in the contract |
| Reversal | Stop running it |

The drafted issue for metalite records the rule and its version, the three
locations, the probe output, both causes of the divergence, and the coverage
statement. It is marked as a dry run and was not submitted.

## Maintain --- Monitor and improve

Four gaps the next cycle must fix: knowledge in one head, runs not comparable,
trigger by memory, recurring triage cost.

### Canonical artifact: Monitoring report

The first cycle's monitoring output is a single decision: the detection logic
works and the delivery mechanism does not. The rule owner accepts the findings
and asks for the procedure to be packaged so that it survives its author.

That accepted decision initiates a second cycle, which is
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill.

## Summary

One prompt found a real divergence, and would also have reported metalite clean
if rounding were assumed to mean `round()`. The value sits in the versioned
site definition, the tie test, and the human decision. The prompt is the least
durable part, which is why the next cycle replaces it.
